title: WhatsApp for Business in Nigeria: Types and How to Use Them
excerpt: The three types of WhatsApp a business can use, which one you need, and how to turn WhatsApp into a reliable way to answer leads and serve clients in Nigeria.
content:
In Nigeria, WhatsApp is usually where the sale actually happens. A customer finds you on Google, Instagram or a friend’s recommendation, and then they message you. How you handle that conversation decides whether you get the job.

WhatsApp works best when new customers can find you first. Our guide on [how to get more customers online](/how-to-get-more-customers) explains how an SEO-ready website and Google profile bring new people into your WhatsApp.

## The three types of WhatsApp

People often ask how many types of WhatsApp there are. For a business, there are three, and they do different jobs.

### 1. WhatsApp (the normal app)

The personal app most people already use. It works, but it gives you nothing that helps a business: no business profile, no catalogue, no automatic replies. Mixing customers with family chats also makes it easy to miss enquiries.

### 2. WhatsApp Business (the free app)

A separate free app from Meta, made for small businesses. You can run it on the same phone as your personal WhatsApp with a different number. It adds:

- a business profile with your address, hours, website and description
- a catalogue for your products or services
- a greeting message for first-time chats and an away message for after hours
- quick replies for answers you type every day
- labels to sort chats, such as “new lead”, “quote sent” and “paid”

For most small businesses in Nigeria, this is the right choice.

### 3. WhatsApp Business Platform (the API)

For larger businesses that need several staff on one number, automated messages, or a connection to their own software. It has no app of its own: you access it through Meta or a provider, and Meta charges for many types of business-initiated messages. Only move to it when the free app genuinely can’t keep up.

## Set up WhatsApp Business properly

- Use a number you’ll keep for years, and use the same number on your website, Google Business Profile and social media. Changing numbers breaks every link and listing that points to you.
- Fill in every profile field: category, description, address or service area, hours, email and website.
- Add your main services or products to the catalogue with prices or “from” prices.
- Write a greeting message that tells people what to send, for example: “Thanks for messaging us. Please send your name, what you need and your location, and we’ll reply within the hour.”
- Set an away message with your working hours.

## How we use WhatsApp at Elevate

We treat our WhatsApp as a professional space for both leads and paying clients. New enquiries and existing clients are answered from the same number, and we label chats so nothing gets lost.

We also work the way each client is comfortable. Some prefer WhatsApp, some prefer email, some prefer another social platform. The channel matters less than replying quickly and keeping a written record of what was agreed.

## Broadcast lists, groups and channels

- **Broadcast lists** send one message to many contacts, but each person receives it as a private chat. Only people who have saved your number receive them, so ask customers to save it.
- **Groups** are conversations where everyone sees everyone. They suit communities, not promotions, and customers leave noisy groups quickly.
- **Channels** are one-way updates that anyone can follow. They are good for announcements and offers, but people have to choose to follow you.

Whichever you use, send less than you think. One useful message a week beats daily flyers that get you muted or reported.

## Connect WhatsApp to your website

Your website and WhatsApp should work together:

- Put a WhatsApp button on every page, especially on phones.
- Use a click-to-chat link (wa.me plus your number) with a pre-filled message, such as “Hi, I found you on your website and I’d like a quote for…”. You’ll know which enquiries came from the site.
- Put the same number on your Google Business Profile so people can message you straight from Google Maps.

## Track what WhatsApp brings in

You don’t need complicated software. Label every new chat with where the person found you (Google, website, Instagram, referral), and count the labels at the end of each month. That simple habit tells you which marketing is working.

## Where WhatsApp stops working

WhatsApp is excellent for conversations, but it can’t bring you new customers who don’t know you exist. That’s the job of your website and Google Business Profile: being found when someone searches for what you sell.

Want customers to find your business before they message you? See our [SEO-ready website design](/services/website-design) or run the [free AI visibility check](/ai-visibility-check) on your current site.

title: How to Choose a Web Design Agency in Nigeria
excerpt: How to choose a web designer or agency in Nigeria: the questions to ask, the red flags behind unfinished projects, and how to make sure the website actually brings customers.
content:
Choosing who builds your website is a bigger decision than it looks. The wrong choice costs more than the fee: months of waiting, a site that never launches, or a site that launches and brings nobody.

You can see how we work in our [case studies](/case-studies).

## The two problems I hear about most

When clients come to us after working with someone else, their stories are usually one of two:

- **The project was never finished.** The developer started, it dragged on for months, communication slowed, and the site was never completed.
- **The site was finished but useless.** It looked fine, but it brought no enquiries. It wasn’t connected to a Google Business Profile, search engines couldn’t properly read it, and it couldn’t be used for marketing. It was just online.

Most of the advice below is about avoiding those two outcomes.

## Get clear on what the site must do

Before you talk to anyone, decide the main job of the website. For most service businesses, it’s marketing: being found by people searching for what you do, and turning them into calls and WhatsApp messages. If the designer only talks about colours and animations, they’re solving a different problem.

## Questions to ask any web designer

- What’s the timeline, and what happens if it runs late?
- How many rounds of changes are included after the first draft?
- Will I own the website code and the domain once it’s paid for? Is that written in the agreement?
- Will each service have its own page?
- Do you set up Google Search Console, Bing, a sitemap and structured data?
- Will you connect the site to my Google Business Profile?
- Can I see live sites you’ve built, and do any of them bring their owners enquiries from Google or ChatGPT?
- Who will I actually talk to during the project?

## Red flags

- No written agreement, or an agreement that doesn’t say who owns the site.
- Full payment upfront with no milestones.
- No live examples, only screenshots or mock-ups.
- Vague timelines like “very soon”.
- Promises of the number 1 position on Google.
- The domain registered in their name, not yours.
- No mention of search engines at all.

## A good quote versus a cheap quote

A good quote lists the pages, what’s included, the timeline, the number of revisions, what happens after launch and what you’ll pay each year. A cheap quote is usually short because it leaves those things out.

## How to check reviews

Look for reviews on Google with real names, and check that the work they mention actually exists online. Open the sites in a portfolio and test them on your phone. Ask to speak to one or two past clients.

## How we handle these

At Elevate, you get a fixed price before work starts, a deposit and balance tied to milestones, a preview link to review the full site before it goes live, and ownership of your site and domain once it’s paid for, written into our agreement. A detailed site usually takes one to two weeks including changes.

When you’re ready, compare our [website design service](/services/website-design) and [fixed prices](/pricing).

title: How Much Does a Website Cost in Nigeria in 2026?
excerpt: Typical website prices in Nigeria in 2026, from basic five-page sites to premium builds, plus domain, hosting and maintenance costs and what to ask before you pay.
content:
Website prices in Nigeria vary more than almost anything else you’ll buy for your business. You can be quoted ₦50,000 by one person and ₦2 million by another for what sounds like the same thing. Here’s what the market looks like in 2026 and how to compare quotes.

Our own fixed prices are on the [pricing page](/pricing).

## Typical prices in 2026

These figures come from published price guides by Nigerian web agencies, so treat them as rough market rates:

- **Basic five-page business website:** around ₦250,000.
- **Growing business website (8 to 10 pages):** around ₦600,000.
- **Premium website (12 to 15 pages, custom design, SEO setup):** around ₦1.5 million.
- **Custom builds with 15+ pages, web apps or online shops:** from about ₦1.8 million, and much more for complex projects.

Very cheap offers usually mean a template with your logo, no copywriting and no SEO setup.

## Ongoing costs

- **Domain:** a .com.ng is cheaper than a .com; a .com usually costs tens of thousands of naira a year, depending on the registrar and exchange rate.
- **Hosting:** from a few thousand naira a month for basic shared hosting to much more for managed hosting.
- **Maintenance:** either your own time every month, or a care plan.

Always ask who owns the domain and hosting account. It should be you.

## What changes the price

- How many pages, and whether each service gets its own page.
- Who writes the words.
- Features: bookings, payments, online shop, client logins.
- Whether search engine setup is included: Google Search Console, Bing, sitemap and structured data.
- How many rounds of changes you get.

## The expensive mistake

The most expensive website is the one that doesn’t bring customers. A cheap site that nobody finds still costs you its price, plus the cost of rebuilding it later. Before comparing prices, read [why websites don’t show up on Google or ChatGPT](/guides/why-your-website-isnt-on-google).

## What we charge

Our Starter Website is ₦250,000 and our Business Website is ₦450,000, both with SEO setup included rather than sold as an extra. A detailed site with several services usually takes one to two weeks, including the changes after the first draft. Full details are on the [pricing page](/pricing).

## Questions to ask before you pay anyone

- Will I own the website and the domain?
- Is search engine setup included, and will the pages be readable without JavaScript?
- Does each service get its own page?
- How long will it take, and how many rounds of changes are included?
- What will I pay every month or year after launch?
- Can I see live sites you’ve built, and speak to those clients?

Comparing with UK prices? See [how much a website costs in the UK in 2026](/guides/website-cost-uk).

Sources: [Kolonell, website cost for SMEs in Lagos 2026](https://kolonell.com/en/blog/how-much-website-costs-sme-lagos-price-guide-2026); [NaijaTechGuide, cost of building a website](https://www.naijatechguide.com/cost-of-building-and-designing-website.html).

title: Your Website Looks Fine but Nobody Contacts You? Here’s Why
excerpt: The most common website complaint: it looks nice, but nobody reaches out. Why it happens, what a website that brings customers needs, and how to measure it.
content:
The complaint I hear most from business owners isn’t about design. It’s this: “My website is fine. It looks nice. But nobody is reaching out.” The site is online, but it isn’t useful.

Not sure if this is happening to you? Run the [free AI visibility check](/ai-visibility-check).

## A website is a marketing tool

Websites have different jobs. An online shop takes payments. But for most service businesses, the main job of a website is marketing. It should be a place where people searching for exactly what you do can find you and reach out, and a steady source of income for the business.

A nice design that nobody finds is money spent for nothing. A good design is the starting point, not the finish line.

## Signs your website is costing you customers

- You can’t remember the last enquiry that came through the website.
- You don’t appear when you search for your main service and your city.
- The site isn’t connected to your Google Business Profile.
- Visitors can’t call or WhatsApp you from the first screen on a phone.
- All your services are squeezed onto one page.
- Prices, hours or services on the site are out of date.
- Nobody can tell you how many people visit the site each month.

## What a website that brings customers has

- **A good design** that looks professional and works on phones first.
- **Good copy** that speaks to your customers’ problems in their words, not just a list of what you do.
- **Your business information in one place, written once and kept consistent:** services, prices, area, hours, phone, WhatsApp and address. Google and AI tools trust details that match everywhere.
- **Pages search engines can read,** one for each service, with answers to the questions customers ask.
- **A clear next step on every page:** call, WhatsApp, book or request a quote.
- **A connection to your Google Business Profile,** so the two support each other.

## Quick fixes that help visitors become enquiries

- Put a WhatsApp button and your phone number at the top of every page.
- Use one main call to action per page, such as “Get a free quote”, and repeat it at the end.
- Show real reviews and real work, with names where clients agree.
- Make forms short: name, phone and what they need is usually enough.
- Make the site load fast on mobile data. Compress images and avoid autoplay video.
- For a campaign or offer, send people to a focused [landing page](/services/landing-pages) instead of your homepage.

## How to measure whether it’s working

You don’t need complicated reports. Track three things:

- **Google Search Console:** how often you appear in search, for which searches, and how many people click.
- **Enquiries by source:** label every new WhatsApp chat or call with where they found you.
- **Simple analytics:** Google Analytics or similar, to see visits and which pages people read.

Compare the enquiries the website brings each month with what it costs you. That’s your return.

## What to do next

If the site gets visitors but no enquiries, fix the copy and the calls to action. If it gets no visitors at all, it’s a findability problem: read [why your website isn’t on Google or ChatGPT](/guides/why-your-website-isnt-on-google).

Our [website redesign service](/services/website-redesign) fixes both without losing the traffic you already have.

title: Website Maintenance Checklist: Weekly, Monthly and Yearly Tasks
excerpt: A practical website maintenance checklist for business owners: what to check every week, month, quarter and year to keep your site live, secure and bringing in enquiries.
content:
A website isn’t finished when it goes live. Links break, forms stop sending, plugins go out of date, and search rankings slip quietly. This checklist covers what to check, and how often, so your site keeps working for you.

If you’d rather not do this yourself, our [website care plans](/services/website-maintenance) cover hosting, updates, backups and checks for a fixed monthly fee.

## Why maintenance matters even when nothing looks broken

Most website problems are silent. The site looks fine to you, but the contact form stopped sending emails two weeks ago, or Google can no longer read a page after an update. You only find out when you notice the enquiries have stopped.

At Elevate, we check our clients’ sites regularly, including clients who aren’t on a monthly plan, to make sure they’re still live and working as intended. It takes minutes, and it catches problems before customers do.

## Weekly checklist

- Open your homepage on your phone. Does it load quickly and look right?
- Send a test message through your contact form and make sure it arrives.
- Tap your WhatsApp and call buttons to confirm they still open correctly.
- Reply to any new Google reviews.

## Monthly checklist

- Update your platform, theme and plugins (for WordPress and similar systems), after taking a backup.
- Check that backups are running and that you could restore one.
- Look at Google Search Console for new errors, pages dropping out of the index, or security warnings.
- Check your most important pages for broken links.
- Update anything out of date: prices, opening hours, team, offers.
- Add at least one new photo or update to your Google Business Profile.

## Quarterly checklist

- Test your site speed with Google PageSpeed Insights and fix the biggest problems.
- Review which pages get impressions and clicks in Search Console, and improve the ones that almost rank.
- Check your business name, phone and address are identical on your website, Google, Facebook and directories.
- Review who has access to your website, hosting and domain, and remove people who no longer need it.

## Yearly checklist

- Renew your domain and SSL certificate before they expire, ideally on auto-renew.
- Review your hosting plan: is it still fast enough and fairly priced?
- Read every page again. Does it still describe what you actually sell today?
- Update your privacy policy if you’ve added new forms, analytics or tools.
- Decide whether the site needs a refresh. See [the signs it’s time for a website redesign](/blog/website-redesign-signs-its-time).

## Modern hosted sites need less, not nothing

Sites built on modern hosting (such as Next.js sites on Vercel, or Wix and Squarespace) don’t have plugins to update, so the security work is lighter. You still need to check forms, content, Search Console, the domain and your Google profile.

## Do it yourself or hand it over?

If you’re comfortable with the checklist and actually do it every month, doing it yourself is fine. Most busy owners don’t, which is why care plans exist. Whatever you choose, put the monthly check in your calendar.

Not sure what search engines can see on your site right now? Run the [free AI visibility check](/ai-visibility-check). UK business? See [SEO websites for UK small businesses](/uk).

title: Local SEO in Nigeria: How to Get Found in Your City in 2026
excerpt: How Nigerian businesses get found on Google Maps, Google search and ChatGPT in their own city: Google Business Profile, service pages, listings, reviews and Bing.
content:
Local SEO means being found by people near you who are searching for what you sell. In Nigeria that matters more every year: DataReportal counted 109 million internet users in Nigeria at the end of 2025, and Google handles almost all searches here.

For the full service, see [local SEO and Google Business Profile optimisation](/services/local-seo).

## How Google decides who shows up

Google says local results are based on three things:

- **Relevance:** how well your business matches what the person searched.
- **Distance:** how close you are to them, or to the place they searched for.
- **Prominence:** how well known you are, based on reviews, links and mentions across the web.

You can’t move your business closer to every customer, but you can work hard on relevance and prominence.

## Step 1: A complete Google Business Profile

Your Google Business Profile is what appears on Google Maps and in the map box above the normal results.

- Choose the primary category that describes what your business is, not everything it does.
- Add every service you offer, using the same names as the service pages on your website.
- Use your real address, or set a service area and hide your address if customers don’t visit you.
- Add real photos of your work, team and premises. Add new ones every month.
- Ask every customer for an honest review, and reply to all of them.

Never put keywords in your business name, use a fake address, or buy reviews. Google suspends profiles for it.

## Step 2: A website Google can read, with a page for each service

Your website gives Google the detail your profile can’t. Each main service needs its own page with your city in the title, a clear description, prices or price ranges, your process and answers to common questions.

The site also has to be readable by search engines. When we first checked the MR DGN Group website, crawlers received 0 readable words, because the content only appeared after JavaScript ran. Read [why websites don’t show up on Google or ChatGPT](/guides/why-your-website-isnt-on-google) for the full list of technical checks.

## Step 3: The same details everywhere

Your business name, phone number and address should be written the same way on your website, Google profile, Facebook and directories. Useful Nigerian listings include VConnect, BusinessList, Finelib and ConnectNigeria, plus Bing Places, Apple Business and Facebook.

## Step 4: Don’t ignore Bing

Bing has a small share of searches in Nigeria, but Bing Places and Bing Webmaster Tools still matter because Bing’s index feeds Microsoft Copilot and other AI search tools. Submitting your site takes a few minutes.

## Step 5: Answer the questions people actually search

Every page that answers a real customer question is another way to be found. Think about the questions you hear on calls and WhatsApp every week: prices, timelines, delivery areas, what’s included. Write a clear answer to each one.

## The opportunity outside Lagos and Abuja

Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt get the most searches, so everyone fights over them. Smaller cities get fewer searches, and most businesses ignore them for that reason. But the people there are still searching. If your business is the one with a complete profile and a clear website, you can win those customers with far less competition.

## What this looks like in practice

MR DGN Construction, a building materials supplier in Asaba, had no Google search presence at all before we started its SEO in March 2026. We rebuilt the site so search engines could read it, added product and service pages, structured data, Search Console and Bing. It now appears in Google search and Google’s AI results every day, and in September 2026 a buyer found the company through ChatGPT and made an enquiry.

We build SEO-ready websites for businesses in every state: see [SEO websites for Nigerian businesses](/locations/nigeria), or start with the [free AI visibility check](/ai-visibility-check).

Sources: [DataReportal, Digital 2026: Nigeria](https://datareportal.com/reports/digital-2026-nigeria); [StatCounter, search engine market share in Nigeria](https://gs.statcounter.com/search-engine-market-share/all/nigeria); [Google Business Profile Help](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091).

title: Mobile-First Design: Why Your Website Must Work on Phones First
excerpt: Google indexes the mobile version of your website, and most of your visitors are on phones. What mobile-first design means and a practical checklist for your site.
content:
Mobile-first design means designing your website for a phone screen first, then adapting it for larger screens, instead of the other way round. It isn’t a trend. It’s how people actually use the web, and how Google reads your site.

Every site in our [website design service](/services/website-design) is designed for phones first.

## Google uses your mobile site

Google uses mobile-first indexing: it mainly crawls and ranks the mobile version of your pages. If content, headings or links are missing on mobile, Google may not see them at all, even if they appear on desktop.

## Your customers are on phones

In Nigeria, DataReportal counted 165 million mobile connections at the end of 2025, and many people browse on mobile data with limited bundles. A heavy page that loads slowly costs them money and patience. In the UK and US, most local searches also happen on phones, often when someone needs a service now.

## What mobile-first looks like in practice

- **The important things first.** On a small screen, the first view should say what you do, where, and how to contact you.
- **Tap-to-call and WhatsApp buttons** that are easy to hit with a thumb.
- **Readable text** without zooming, with enough space between lines and buttons.
- **Light pages.** Compressed images, no autoplay video, and as little code as possible.
- **Short forms.** Typing on a phone is slow, so ask only for what you need.
- **The same content on mobile and desktop.** Don’t hide important text on phones.
- **Menus that work** with one hand and don’t cover the page.

## A five-minute test

- Open your site on a mid-range Android phone, on mobile data, not Wi-Fi.
- Time how long the first screen takes to appear.
- Try to call or WhatsApp the business in two taps.
- Fill in the contact form.
- Run the page through Google PageSpeed Insights and look at the mobile score.

If any of these are frustrating for you, they’re worse for a customer who doesn’t know your business yet.

## Next step

See real examples in our [case studies](/case-studies), or read the [signs it’s time for a website redesign](/blog/website-redesign-signs-its-time).

Sources: [Google Search Central, mobile-first indexing best practices](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/mobile/mobile-sites-mobile-first-indexing); [DataReportal, Digital 2026: Nigeria](https://datareportal.com/reports/digital-2026-nigeria).

title: SEO Basics for Small Business Owners: A Plain-English Guide
excerpt: What SEO actually means for a small business, how Google decides what to show, and the basics you can check yourself, explained without jargon.
content:
SEO (search engine optimisation) sounds technical, but the idea is simple: make it easy for Google, and now AI tools like ChatGPT, to understand your business and show it to people searching for what you sell.

Want to see where your site stands first? Run the [free AI visibility check](/ai-visibility-check).

## How search works, in one example

Think about how you search TikTok, Instagram or YouTube for a video you saw a while ago. You type a few words, and the app pieces together what you typed with what it has, and shows its best guess. It wants you to find what you’re looking for, so you keep using it.

Google works the same way. It looks at what the person typed, where they are, and which pages best answer it. SEO is making sure your page is the best answer, and that Google can read it.

## The basics every small business needs

- **A website Google can read.** The text should be in the page itself, not loaded later by JavaScript. Many sites look fine to people but send search engines an almost empty page.
- **One page per service.** If everything sits on one page, Google has little to match. A page for each service gives each search a clear answer.
- **Clear titles.** Each page title should say what the page is about and, for local businesses, where: “Roof Repairs in Abuja” beats “Home”.
- **Answers to real questions.** Write down the questions customers ask before they buy, and answer them on your pages.
- **Contact details on every page.** Phone, WhatsApp and location, written the same way everywhere.
- **Google Search Console and Bing.** Submit your site and sitemap so search engines know every page exists.
- **A Google Business Profile.** For local businesses, this is how you appear on Google Maps.

## What doesn’t work

- Stuffing the same keyword into every sentence.
- Copying text from other websites, or publishing lots of thin pages.
- Buying links or fake reviews.
- Anyone who guarantees the number 1 position on Google.

## How long SEO takes

Fixing the technical basics can help within weeks. Steady rankings usually take a few months of consistent work, depending on your industry and city. In smaller towns with less competition, it can be faster.

## Your next step

For the next step, read [how to get more customers online](/how-to-get-more-customers), or if your site doesn’t show up at all, [why your website isn’t on Google or ChatGPT](/guides/why-your-website-isnt-on-google). If you want it done for you, see our [local SEO service](/services/local-seo).

title: 7 Signs It’s Time for a Website Redesign
excerpt: Seven clear signs your website needs a redesign, from no enquiries to a builder search engines can’t read, and how to redesign without losing your Google rankings.
content:
A redesign isn’t about following trends. It’s worth doing when your current site is stopping customers from finding you or contacting you. Here are the signs I look for.

If several of these sound familiar, see how our [website redesign service](/services/website-redesign) rebuilds sites without losing what already ranks.

## 1. It brings no enquiries

The clearest sign. If the site has been live for months and you can’t point to customers it brought you, something is wrong: either nobody finds it, or the people who find it don’t act. See [why a website that looks fine can still cost you customers](/blog/your-website-is-costing-you-customers).

## 2. Search engines can’t read it

Some sites look perfect to people but send search engines almost nothing, because the text only appears after JavaScript runs. This is common with sites made by some AI builders and older single-page app templates. Read [Lovable, Wix and Squarespace sites not showing on Google](/guides/lovable-wix-squarespace-seo).

## 3. It doesn’t work well on phones

Most visitors are on phones. If they have to pinch and zoom, wait for slow pages, or hunt for your number, they leave. Google also uses the mobile version of your site for indexing. More on that in [why mobile-first design isn’t optional](/blog/mobile-first-design).

## 4. All your services are on one page

One “Services” page with a list gives Google little to match. Each main service needs its own page with its own title, details and answers to common questions.

## 5. You can’t update it yourself, or you don’t know who can

If changing a price means chasing a developer who no longer answers, the site will go out of date. You should own your site and domain, and have a clear way to get changes made.

## 6. Your previous developer never finished it

This is one of the most common stories I hear: a developer started the project, it dragged on for months, and it was never completed. Half-finished pages, placeholder text and broken links hurt trust with customers and with Google.

## 7. It looks out of date next to your competitors

Design does matter for trust. If your site looks older than the businesses you compete with, visitors assume the business is too. Old photos, outdated prices and a copyright year from five years ago all send that message.

## How to redesign without losing your rankings

A redesign can wipe out the visibility you already have if it’s done carelessly. Before you rebuild:

- List every page that gets impressions or clicks in Google Search Console.
- Keep those page addresses the same where you can.
- Redirect any old address that changes to its new page (a 301 redirect).
- Keep the content that ranks, and improve it rather than deleting it.
- Submit the new sitemap and check Search Console for errors after launch.

Find out in seconds whether search engines can read your current site with the [free AI visibility check](/ai-visibility-check).
